"Blow away" is a phrasal verb. A phrasal verb is a regular verb (like blow, give, take) combined with one or two small words (like away, up, off) to create a completely new meaning. The new meaning is often very different from the original verb, so you cannot guess it just by knowing the main verb.

"Blow away" has one literal meaning and three major figurative meanings. You need to know all of them because native speakers use all of them regularly.
The Literal Meaning — Wind Physically Moving Something

"Blow away" means wind or air forcefully moves something from one place to another, or carries it out of sight.

Think of what happens on a windy day. A gust of wind picks up a paper from a table and carries it off. That paper gets blown away. The wind is the active force that "blows" the object, and "away" tells you the object moves from where it was to somewhere else — or disappears entirely.

Examples:

  • "The wind blew my umbrella away." (The wind took the umbrella from my hands and carried it off.)
  • "My papers blew away before I could grab them."
  • "The kite blew away and we couldn't find it."

Notice that the subject is always wind, air, a fan, or some similar force. This is the key sign that the phrase is being used literally.
Figurative Meaning #1 — To Deeply Impress or Amaze Someone

This is the most common and most important meaning you will encounter. When something "blows you away," it impresses, amazes, or overwhelms you so powerfully that you are almost speechless. It goes far beyond ordinary liking or admiring — it describes a feeling of being completely stunned by how good, beautiful, or powerful something is.

Think of it this way: imagine you are a piece of paper sitting on a table. Something so impressive comes along that it hits you like a giant gust of wind — so strong that it "blows you away." You are no longer standing where you were. You are completely moved.

Examples:

  • "Her singing blew me away. I didn't expect it to be that good."
  • "The special effects in that film completely blew me away."
  • "I was blown away by how kind everyone was."
  • "The view from the top of the mountain blew us all away."

Important grammar note — active vs. passive:

You will see this meaning in two forms, and both are very common:

In the active form, something impresses you: "The concert blew me away."
In the passive form, you are the one feeling amazed: "I was blown away by the concert."

The passive form ("I was blown away") is actually extremely common in everyday speech. You will hear it all the time. Both forms mean the same thing.

Important nuance: This meaning always implies a positive, wonderful kind of shock. Something is so much better than you expected that your reaction is bigger than normal surprise — it's genuine awe.
Figurative Meaning #2 — To Defeat Someone Very Easily and Completely

"Blow away" can also mean to beat or defeat someone so decisively that there is no real competition. It is not a close win. The winner dominates so completely that the loser barely stands a chance. The idea is that the winner "blows away" the competition the way wind scatters dry leaves — effortlessly and completely.

Examples:

  • "Our team blew away the competition and finished first by a huge margin."
  • "She blew away all the other applicants in the interview."
  • "The new phone blew away every competitor in the speed tests."
  • "He blew the other runners away and crossed the finish line 10 seconds ahead."

How to recognize this meaning: Look for context involving a contest, competition, race, comparison, or test. When one side wins very easily, "blew away" is a natural choice.
Figurative Meaning #3 — To Completely Eliminate a Doubt, Fear, or Worry

When "blow away" is used with abstract nouns like doubt, fear, worry, concern, or myth, it means to completely destroy or eliminate those feelings or beliefs. Something comes along and removes those negative things entirely, just like a strong wind clears away fog or smoke.

Examples:

  • "His explanation blew away all my doubts about the plan."
  • "One conversation with her blew away all my fears."
  • "The study blew away the myth that drinking coffee is always bad for you."
  • "Seeing the place in person blew away my concerns."

How to recognize this meaning: Look for emotional or mental things — doubts, fears, myths, misconceptions — being "blown away." The context will feel more thoughtful and analytical than emotional.
Figurative Meaning #4 — To Kill Someone (Informal / Slang)

In informal, colloquial English — especially in crime stories, action movies, and casual conversation about violence — "blow away" can mean to shoot and kill someone. This is slang, and it is graphic and blunt in tone.

Examples:

  • "The villain blew away the guard and escaped."
  • "In the movie, the detective nearly gets blown away in the final scene."

Important warning: This meaning is not appropriate for formal writing or professional settings. It belongs to informal speech, fiction, films, and news reporting about crime. If you are a learner, you do not need to use this meaning yourself — but you need to recognize it so you understand what people mean in films, books, and casual conversation.
How the Grammar Works — A Closer Look

Understanding how to use "blow away" correctly is just as important as knowing what it means.

"Blow away" is a separable phrasal verb. This means that when there is an object (the thing or person being blown away), you can either keep the phrase together or split it:

  • "The storm blew away the tent." (together)
  • "The storm blew the tent away." (split — also correct)

Both of these are perfectly natural. However, when you use a pronoun (like it, me, him, them), you must split the phrase and put the pronoun in the middle:

  • ✅ "The concert blew me away."
  • ❌ "The concert blew away me." (This is wrong and sounds unnatural.)

So, always remember: pronoun goes in the middle, noun can go either way.

Tense forms you will commonly see:

  • Present: "This movie blows me away every single time I watch it."
  • Past: "Her performance blew everyone away."
  • Past participle (passive): "I was blown away by her performance."
  • Present participle: "This landscape is truly blowing me away right now."
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Since "blow away" has multiple meanings, context is your best guide. Ask yourself these questions:

Is there actual wind or air involved? → Literal meaning (wind moving something).

Is someone talking about being amazed or deeply impressed by something? → Figurative Meaning #1 (to impress).

Is there a competition, race, test, or comparison? → Figurative Meaning #2 (to defeat easily).

Are doubts, fears, myths, or concerns being mentioned? → Figurative Meaning #3 (to eliminate).

Is there violence, a gun, or a crime context? → Figurative Meaning #4 (to kill).
Register — When and Where Is This Phrase Used?

"Blow away" is informal to neutral in register. It is perfectly natural in everyday conversation, casual writing, social media, journalism, and fiction. You would not normally use it in a formal academic essay or a legal document, but in almost every other situation, it is completely appropriate.

The one exception is Meaning #4 (to kill) — that one is strictly informal and should only be used in casual or creative contexts.
A Final Summary to Lock It In

The phrase "blow away" works in four layers. Literally, wind carries something off. Figuratively, something can "blow you away" by impressing you enormously, a winner can "blow away" the competition by defeating them easily, or new information can "blow away" your doubts by removing them completely. In slang, it can also mean to kill. The passive form "blown away" — as in "I was blown away" — is especially common and important to remember. Context, always, is what tells you which meaning is being used.
1901:
When someone "blows their own trumpet," it means they are praising themselves, boasting about their own achievements, or drawing attention to how great they are — usually in a way that other people find annoying or unnecessary.

In simple words: it means to show off about yourself.

"He's always blowing his own trumpet about how many medals he has won."

This means: He constantly brags about his medals.
Where Did This Idiom Come From?

To understand this idiom deeply, picture this scene from hundreds of years ago:

In ancient and medieval times, when a king, queen, or an important warrior arrived at a ceremony or public gathering, a trumpeter (a person whose job was to play the trumpet) would blow the trumpet loudly. This was a signal to everyone around: "Pay attention! Someone important is here!"

So, someone else always blew the trumpet for you. It was a great honor to have another person announce your arrival that way.

Now imagine if, instead of waiting for someone else to do it, you grabbed the trumpet and blew it yourself — announcing your own importance. That would be seen as shameless and arrogant, because you are essentially telling the whole world how great you are, without being asked.

That is exactly what the idiom captures. Blowing your own trumpet means you are not waiting for others to praise you — you are doing it yourself, loudly and publicly.

The idiom has been in use in the English language since at least the 16th century and remains widely used today, especially in British English.
The Tone: Is It Always Negative?

Most of the time, calling someone out for blowing their own trumpet carries a mildly negative or disapproving tone. It suggests the person is being:

  • Boastful — talking too proudly about themselves
  • Self-centered — making conversations about their own greatness
  • Socially unaware — not realizing that others find it tiresome

However, the idiom is not always harsh. Sometimes it is used in a light, self-aware, or even humble way. People often use it to warn you before they share something good about themselves, almost as if apologizing for it:

"I don't mean to blow my own trumpet, but I did finish the project two weeks ahead of schedule."

Here, the speaker is acknowledging that what they're about to say sounds like bragging, but they feel it's important to mention. This use is polite and self-deprecating (meaning they are gently making fun of themselves).

Here are several example sentences showing the idiom in different situations:

  1. Negative use (disapproval):
    "My cousin never stops blowing his own trumpet. Every dinner, he talks about how successful he is."
  2. Neutral/self-aware use:
    "I don't like to blow my own trumpet, but I was the only one in the room who spotted the error."
  3. Talking about someone else's modesty (reverse use):
    "She never blows her own trumpet, even though she has achieved more than anyone else on the team."
    (Here, it's actually a compliment — she is praised for NOT bragging.)
  4. In a workplace setting:
    "During the interview, don't be afraid to blow your own trumpet a little — employers want to know what makes you special."
    (Here, it is used encouragingly — some self-promotion is actually useful.)

This idiom is most common in British English. If you are speaking or reading American English, the same idea is usually expressed as:

  • "Toot one's own horn" — "He's always tooting his own horn about his salary."
  • "Blow one's own horn" — a less common but valid American variation.

All three mean exactly the same thing. The only difference is regional preference.

These idioms and phrases carry a very similar meaning and are worth knowing alongside this one:

  • "Sing one's own praises" — "She was busy singing her own praises all evening."
  • "Pat oneself on the back" — "He patted himself on the back for closing the deal." (slightly milder — more about self-congratulation than public boasting)
  • "Show off" — a simpler, more direct way to say the same thing.
  • "Brag" or "Boast" — single-word equivalents.
A Quick Way to Remember It

Think of it this way:

A trumpet is loud and impossible to ignore. When someone blows their own trumpet, they are being just as loud and impossible to ignore — except the noise they're making is about how wonderful they are.

If you remember that image — a person literally standing up and blowing a trumpet to announce themselves — the meaning of this idiom will never leave you.
"Blow one's own trumpet" = to boast about your own abilities or achievements, often in a way that others find annoying or unnecessary.
1902:
To blow something out of proportion means to treat a small or minor problem as if it were much bigger, more serious, or more important than it actually is. In other words, it means to exaggerate or overreact to something.

Think of it this way: if a small ant walked into your house, you would normally just squash it or ignore it. But if you called an exterminator, told all your neighbors, cancelled your vacation, and refused to sleep at home — that reaction is wildly bigger than the problem deserves. You would be blowing the situation out of proportion.
Breaking Down the Words

Understanding the individual words helps you understand why the idiom means what it means.

"Proportion" means the correct or appropriate size or importance of something relative to other things. When something is "in proportion," it means the reaction or response matches the actual size of the situation. For example, if a tiny problem gets a tiny reaction — that's proportionate. If a tiny problem gets a massive, dramatic reaction — that's out of proportion.

"Blow" here is used informally to mean to inflate, puff up, or make something larger than it is — much like blowing air into a balloon to make it expand. The balloon (the problem) was originally small, but after you "blow" it, it appears much bigger.

So, when you put them together: to blow something out of proportion = to puff a small thing up until it looks much bigger and more serious than it really is.
The Simple Formula

Reality of the situation + Exaggerated reaction = Something blown out of proportion.

The gap between how serious a situation actually is and how seriously someone treats it is what this idiom captures.
Grammar: How to Use It

This idiom is a verb phrase. The key verb is "blow," and it changes form depending on the tense you use. The word "something" (the object — the thing being exaggerated) goes between "blow" and "out of proportion."

Here are the grammatical patterns:

Active voice (someone is doing the exaggerating):

  • Subject + blow/blows/blew/is blowing + object + out of proportion
  • "She is blowing this argument out of proportion."
  • "He blew the whole incident out of proportion."
  • "Stop blowing things out of proportion."

Passive voice (the focus is on the thing being exaggerated):

  • Object + is/was/has been blown + out of proportion
  • "This issue has been blown completely out of proportion."
  • "The story was blown out of proportion by the media."

Without an object (general statement):

  • "You always blow things out of proportion."
  • "Don't blow it out of proportion."
Real-Life Examples (From Easy to Complex)

Example 1 — A small mistake at work:

"I made one spelling error in an email, and my manager called an emergency meeting about it. He completely blew it out of proportion."

Reality: A minor typo. Reaction: An emergency meeting. Huge gap = blown out of proportion.

Example 2 — A friendship argument:

"Anna and I had a tiny disagreement about where to eat lunch, but she stopped talking to me for a whole week. I think she blew it out of proportion."

Example 3 — Health anxiety:

"I had a mild headache, but I convinced myself I had a serious illness and went to three different hospitals. My doctor told me I was blowing it out of proportion."

Example 4 — Media or news:

"A local storm caused minor flooding in one street, but the news channels made it sound like the whole city was underwater. The situation was blown completely out of proportion."

Example 5 — Self-reflection (used on yourself):

"Okay, I know I'm blowing this out of proportion. My presentation went fine. One person yawning doesn't mean everyone hated it."

This last example is important — people can use this idiom to criticize their own overreaction, not just someone else's.
Common Variations of the Idiom

The idiom appears in slightly different forms. All of them mean the same thing:

  • "Blow something out of all proportion" — Adding "all" makes it sound even more extreme. Very commonly used in British English.
    • "The story has been blown out of all proportion."
  • "Blown out of proportion" — The passive, past participle form. Very frequently used.
    • "This is being blown out of proportion."
  • "Blowing things out of proportion" — A general, habitual way of saying someone always overreacts.
    • "He has a habit of blowing things out of proportion."

All these variations are natural and widely accepted.
Tone and When to Use It

This idiom carries a critical or corrective tone. When you say someone is blowing something out of proportion, you are essentially saying:

"Your reaction is too big for the size of this problem. Calm down. You are not seeing this clearly."

It can be said:

  • To someone else as a gentle correction or mild criticism.
  • About someone else when describing their behavior to a third person.
  • About yourself as honest self-awareness.

It is used in both formal and informal contexts, though it is more common in everyday conversation, journalism, and social discussions than in highly technical or academic writing.
What It Does NOT Mean

Do not confuse this idiom with simply "exaggerating" in a storytelling sense. For example, if someone says, "I've told you a million times!" — that's a casual exaggeration for effect, but it isn't really blowing something out of proportion in the idiom's sense.

"Blowing out of proportion" specifically refers to treating a real situation or problem as far more serious or important than it deserves — it's about the emotional or social reaction being disproportionate to the actual event.
Similar Idioms With the Same Meaning

Knowing related idioms deepens your understanding and gives you more tools to express this idea:

  • "Make a mountain out of a molehill" — Turning a tiny problem (a molehill) into a huge one (a mountain). Very close in meaning.
  • "Make a big deal out of nothing" — Treating something unimportant as very significant.
  • "Storm in a teacup" (British English) — A big fuss or overreaction about something trivial.
  • "Overreact" — The single-word verb equivalent. Less colorful, but the same idea.
A Quick Memory Trick

Picture a balloon. Now imagine blowing air into it far beyond its normal size until it looks huge and ready to pop. The balloon hasn't changed — it's the same balloon — but your blowing has made it look enormous and dangerous.

That balloon is the problem. The blowing is the exaggerated reaction. Together, they create something "blown out of proportion."
Summary in One Sentence
"Blow out of proportion" means to react to, or describe, something as far more serious or important than it actually is — to exaggerate a situation to a degree that does not match reality.
1903: "Blow over" has two meanings: one literal (physical/real-world) and one figurative (metaphorical). The figurative meaning is the one you will encounter most in everyday life, but understanding the literal meaning first will help you "see" where the phrase comes from.
1. The Literal Meaning — When Wind Knocks Something Down

In its most basic, physical sense, "blow over" means the wind knocks something down or tips it over.

Think of a strong wind hitting a tree, a fence, or a trash can on the street. The wind blows it, and it falls over. That physical action — wind + something falling/tipping — is the literal meaning.

Examples:

  • "The storm was so strong that it blew over several trees." (The wind knocked the trees down.)
  • "My umbrella blew over in the wind." (The wind knocked my umbrella flat.)
  • "Be careful — a gust of wind could blow that sign over."

This meaning is straightforward and visual. If you can picture a lamppost being knocked sideways by a heavy wind, you understand it completely.
2. The Figurative Meaning — When a Problem or Bad Situation Passes

This is the meaning you will use and hear most often. When a problem, conflict, argument, scandal, or difficult situation "blows over," it means it gradually fades away, calms down, or comes to an end on its own — without leaving serious, lasting damage.

Think of a thunderstorm. Dark clouds come, there is thunder and lightning, things feel tense and scary — but then, the clouds blow over (pass across the sky and move on), the rain stops, and the sky becomes calm and clear again. The storm didn't last forever. It passed.

This is exactly the image the figurative meaning borrows. A difficult situation — like a storm — is temporary. It will pass. It will blow over.

Examples:

  • "Don't worry about the argument you had with your friend. These things always blow over." (The argument will fade and be forgotten.)
  • "The politician was embarrassed by the scandal, but it blew over within a month." (The scandal faded from people's attention over time.)
  • "He was angry at me, but I waited for his anger to blow over before I spoke to him again." (His anger gradually calmed down.)
  • "The controversy about the company's decision eventually blew over." (People stopped talking about it and moved on.)
Where Does the Phrase Come From?

The phrase comes directly from nature — specifically, from weather. For thousands of years, people watched storms form and pass. When a storm or strong wind passes over an area and continues moving, the people in that area say the storm "blew over." This eventually became a metaphor for any difficult situation that passes without permanently destroying things, just like a storm that passes without destroying everything in its path.
The Key Idea Behind the Figurative Meaning

There are three core ideas packed into "blow over" when used figuratively:

1. Time — The situation doesn't resolve instantly. It takes some time, but it eventually ends.

2. Natural resolution — The situation usually resolves on its own, rather than because of a dramatic action by someone. It simply fades, like a storm that eventually moves on.

3. No permanent damage — The situation may have been difficult or uncomfortable, but it does not cause a permanent, life-changing problem. It comes and goes.
Grammar — How Is It Used?

"Blow over" is a phrasal verb — a phrase made of a verb ("blow") and a small word ("over") that together create a specific meaning.

Pattern 1: Intransitive (No Object — Most Common in the Figurative Sense)

Here, nothing receives the action. The situation itself just "blows over."

Structure: Subject + blow over

  • "This will blow over."
  • "The argument has blown over."
  • "I hope the trouble blows over soon."

Pattern 2: Transitive (With an Object — More Common in the Literal Sense)

Here, something is acted upon — the wind knocks a specific object down.

Structure: Subject + blow + object + over OR Subject + blow over + object

  • "The wind blew the fence over." ✅
  • "The wind blew over the fence." ✅

Both word orders are correct in the literal sense. In everyday speech, the object usually goes between "blow" and "over" when the object is a noun ("blew the fence over"), and "over" comes right after "blow" if the object comes later.

Common Tenses You Will Hear

TenseExample

Future tense is the most common — people use "blow over" to comfort someone or predict that a problem will pass.

  • "Don't worry, it will blow over."
  • "This crisis will blow over eventually."

Past tense is also very common — describing a situation that has already passed.

  • "The scandal blew over after a few weeks."
  • "The argument finally blew over."

Present perfect is used to say something has just recently resolved.

  • "I think things have blown over now. You can talk to him."
The Tone of "Blow Over"

The phrase almost always carries an optimistic or reassuring tone. When someone says "it will blow over," they are usually trying to comfort someone — telling them not to panic, because the situation is temporary.

  • "You had a bad day at work? Don't stress — it'll blow over."
  • "The media is covering this story now, but it'll blow over."

However, it can sometimes carry a slightly dismissive tone, if someone uses it to suggest that a serious problem is less important than it really is.

  • "The prime minister said the protests would blow over — but they didn't." (Here, the phrase implies he was wrong to minimize the situation.)

So context matters. It can be comforting, or it can sound like someone is not taking something seriously enough.
When Should You Use "Blow Over"?

Use it when:

  • A conflict or argument between people will likely fade with time ("Your fight with your brother will blow over.")
  • A scandal or controversy loses public attention ("The company's PR crisis eventually blew over.")
  • Someone's anger or upset feelings gradually calm down ("Let her calm down. Her frustration will blow over.")
  • A period of stress, difficulty, or trouble passes ("The rough patch in their marriage blew over.")
  • A literal storm passes over an area ("The storm will blow over by morning.")
When Should You NOT Use "Blow Over"?

Do not use it for situations that are permanent, catastrophic, or unlikely to simply fade on their own. It would sound strange or even offensive to use it for things like terminal illness, permanent financial ruin, or irreversible disasters — because the phrase carries the implication that "everything will be fine," which is not appropriate for every situation.
Common Phrases You Will Hear It In

• "It'll blow over." — The single most common use. A quick reassurance.
  • "Wait for it to blow over." — Advising patience.
  • "Once the storm blows over..." — This cleverly mixes the literal and figurative meanings together.
  • "Things will blow over eventually." — A general prediction that the situation will improve with time.
  • "I thought it would blow over, but it didn't." — Expressing that a situation turned out to be more serious than expected.
Synonyms — Other Ways to Say the Same Thing

If you want to express the same idea with different words, you can use:

  • "pass" — "This problem will pass."
  • "fade away" — "The controversy will fade away."
  • "die down" — "The anger will die down."
  • "fizzle out" — "The drama will fizzle out."
  • "calm down" — "Things will calm down."
  • "peter out" — "The public interest will peter out."

However, none of these carry the same vivid, storm-weather imagery that "blow over" does, which is why it remains a uniquely expressive and popular phrase.
Quick Summary

AspectDetail

Literal meaning: Wind physically knocks something down.

Figurative meaning (main use): A difficult situation — an argument, scandal, crisis, or tension — gradually fades and ends on its own without causing permanent damage.

Tone: Usually reassuring and optimistic; occasionally dismissive.

Grammar: Mostly used intransitively in the figurative sense (no object needed — the situation simply "blows over").

Origin: From the image of a storm passing over the sky and moving on, leaving calm behind.

Most common form: "It will blow over" or "It'll blow over."

The beauty of this phrase is that it takes one simple, universal image from nature — a storm that comes and goes — and turns it into a way to talk about all of life's difficult moments that are temporary. Once you see the storm image in your mind, you will never forget what "blow over" means.
1904:
To "blow the whistle" means to expose or report someone's wrongdoing, dishonesty, or illegal activity — usually to a person in authority or to the public.

When someone "blows the whistle," they are revealing a secret that someone powerful was trying to hide, often at personal risk to themselves.

Think of it this way: imagine you work at a company and you discover that your boss is secretly stealing money from customers. If you go to the police or the media and tell them what's happening — that is blowing the whistle.

The idiom comes from real whistles — the kind referees and police officers use.

When a referee in a sports game sees a player break the rules, they blow a whistle to stop the game and signal that something is wrong. Similarly, when a police officer spots a crime happening in the street, they blow a whistle to raise an alarm and call attention to it.

So the idea carried into everyday language: just like a whistle-blower in sports or policing calls out bad behavior and stops it, a person who "blows the whistle" in real life exposes bad behavior that was happening in secret.

The expression became especially common in the 20th century, particularly in the context of business, politics, and government, where corruption and wrongdoing often happen behind closed doors.
The Key Elements of This Idiom

To really understand this idiom deeply, notice these three things that are always true when someone "blows the whistle":

1. There is a wrongdoing happening.
Something unfair, illegal, dangerous, or unethical is going on — a fraud, a crime, a cover-up, a safety violation, etc.

2. Someone finds out about it.
The person who blows the whistle usually has inside knowledge — they are often an employee, a colleague, or someone who is part of the group committing the wrongdoing.

3. They choose to reveal it.
They report it to an authority (like the police, a regulator, or management) or go public (like telling a journalist or the public directly), even though this might put them in danger.
The Person Who Does It: A "Whistleblower"

The person who blows the whistle is called a whistleblower (one word). This is a very common and widely used term in English, especially in news and journalism.

Whistleblowers are often seen as brave but vulnerable people. They expose the truth, but they frequently face serious consequences for doing so — like losing their job, being sued, or even being threatened. This is why "blowing the whistle" carries a sense of courage and risk.

Some of the most famous real-life whistleblowers in history include:

  • Edward Snowden, who revealed that the US government was secretly spying on millions of ordinary citizens around the world.
  • Daniel Ellsberg, who leaked secret government documents about the Vietnam War to newspapers.
  • Frances Haugen, a Facebook employee who revealed internal documents showing the company knew its platforms were causing harm.

All of these people "blew the whistle" on powerful institutions.
How to Use It in a Sentence

The most common structures are:

"Blow the whistle on [someone/something]" — this is the most frequent form.

  • She decided to blow the whistle on her company's illegal dumping of chemicals.
  • He was fired after blowing the whistle on the corrupt managers.
  • It took courage for her to blow the whistle on the fraud.

"Blow the whistle" — used without "on" when the context is already clear.

  • He knew about the wrongdoing for years before he finally blew the whistle.
  • If no one blows the whistle, the corruption will continue forever.

This idiom is generally used in a serious, often admirable context. When we say someone "blew the whistle," we usually mean it as a positive or neutral description — they did something brave and honest.

However, occasionally it can be used slightly negatively, if the person is seen as a traitor by their group — for example, in a gang or a corrupt organization, being a "whistleblower" could be considered betrayal. But in mainstream society and standard English usage, the word carries a heroic or courageous tone.

It is not used for trivial things. You would NOT say "She blew the whistle on her friend for eating her sandwich." The idiom is reserved for significant wrongdoing — crimes, corruption, dangerous cover-ups, serious ethical violations.

This idiom is used in both formal and informal contexts:

  • In newspapers and news broadcasts, you will see it constantly: "The whistleblower who exposed the scandal..."
  • In everyday conversation, people use it naturally: "Someone finally blew the whistle on that corrupt politician."
  • In legal and business contexts, the word "whistleblower" is even used in official laws. Many countries have whistleblower protection laws that legally protect people who report wrongdoing from being punished by their employers.

Knowing related phrases helps you see the full picture:

  • "Rat someone out" — an informal, somewhat negative way to say the same thing (but sounds more like a betrayal).
  • "Tip off" — to give secret information to someone (usually the police or authorities), but this is more neutral and doesn't always involve exposing wrongdoing.
  • "Expose" — a direct, literal synonym. To expose someone's wrongdoing is the same action, just without the idiom.
  • "Speak out" — to publicly say something controversial or difficult. Similar feeling of bravery, but broader — you can "speak out" about anything, not just a specific wrongdoing.
  • "Come forward" — to step forward and share information, often used in the context of witnesses.

Picture a referee on a football field. The players (corrupt officials, dishonest bosses, criminal organizations) are breaking the rules, thinking no one will notice. Then one brave person stands up, puts the whistle to their lips, and blows it loudly — stopping everything and calling out the wrongdoing for everyone to see.

That image is the idiom. Carry it with you, and you'll never forget it.
"Blow the whistle" means to bravely expose or report someone's serious wrongdoing — especially when that person is powerful and the truth was being hidden.
1905:
"Blow up" is a phrasal verb. A phrasal verb is a combination of a verb (a doing word) and one or more small words (like "up," "out," or "in") that together create a new meaning — often very different from the original verb alone. For example, "blow" by itself means to push air out of your mouth or for wind to move. But when you add "up," the meaning changes completely — in fact, it changes in several different ways depending on the situation.

This is what makes phrasal verbs both interesting and tricky: one combination of words can carry many different meanings. "Blow up" is a perfect example of that.

Meaning 1: To Explode (or to Destroy Something with an Explosion)

This is the most literal meaning. When something blows up, it explodes — usually with fire, force, and a loud sound.

"The old factory blew up after a gas leak."

You can also use it in an active way, where someone causes the explosion:

"The army blew up the bridge so the enemy couldn't cross it."

Key point: In the first sentence, the factory itself exploded (no one is doing it on purpose). In the second sentence, the army made it explode. Both are correct uses of "blow up," just with different subjects.

Meaning 2: To Fill Something with Air

When you blow up a balloon, a tyre, or an inflatable mattress, you are filling it with air to make it expand.

"Can you help me blow up these balloons for the party?"
"He stopped at the petrol station to blow up the tyres."

This meaning is very close to the physical action of blowing — pushing air — so it is easier to remember.

Meaning 3: To Suddenly Become Very Angry

This is one of the most common informal uses. When a person blows up, they suddenly lose their temper and become very angry — often loudly.

"She blew up at her colleague for taking credit for her work."
"I tried to stay calm, but eventually I just blew up."

You can also say someone blew up at a person (to show who received the anger):

"My dad blew up at me when he saw my exam results."

Think of it like a pressure cooker: emotions build up inside, and then — like an explosion — they burst out suddenly. That is where the image comes from.

Meaning 4: To Enlarge a Photo or Image

When you blow up a photograph or image, you make it bigger — you enlarge it.

"The detective asked the technician to blow up the photo so they could see the suspect's face more clearly."
"Can you blow up this section of the image? I can't read the text."

This meaning likely comes from the darkroom days of photography, when "blowing up" a negative meant projecting and enlarging it onto paper.

Meaning 5: To Suddenly Become Very Famous or Successful

In modern informal English — especially in music, social media, and pop culture — when a person, a song, or a brand blows up, it becomes very popular or famous very quickly, often almost overnight.

"That rapper was completely unknown last year, but he blew up after one song went viral."
"Her business blew up after she appeared on television."
"That video blew up on the internet and got 20 million views in one week."

This meaning is especially common among younger speakers and in conversations about social media and entertainment.

Meaning 6: To Fail Suddenly and Completely

When a plan, a relationship, a deal, or a situation blows up, it collapses or falls apart — usually suddenly and badly.

"The merger between the two companies blew up at the last minute."
"Their friendship blew up over a misunderstanding."
"Everything was going well, and then the whole project just blew up."

Notice that in this meaning, nothing literally explodes — but the idea of something suddenly breaking apart in a destructive way is the same as an explosion.

Meaning 7: To Make Something Seem Bigger or More Important Than It Is (To Exaggerate)

When someone — often the media or a person — blows up a story, event, or issue, they exaggerate it or give it far more attention than it perhaps deserves.

"The newspapers really blew up that story — it wasn't as serious as they made it sound."
"He blew up a small argument into a massive drama."

You will also hear the related expression "blown out of proportion," which means the same idea: something small has been made to seem enormous.

Meaning 8: Someone's Phone Is "Blowing Up"

In everyday modern English, if someone's phone is blowing up, it means they are receiving a very large number of calls, texts, or notifications in a short time — constantly buzzing or ringing.

"Ever since she posted that photo, her phone has been blowing up with messages."
"My phone is blowing up — something must have happened."

You can also say someone is blowing up your phone, meaning they are calling or messaging you repeatedly:

"He's been blowing up my phone all morning. I'll call him back later."
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Because "blow up" has so many meanings, you might wonder: How do I know which one is being used? The answer is context — the surrounding words and situation almost always make it clear.

Here is how to think about it:

  • If someone is talking about a bomb, a building, or a gas leak → explosion.
  • If someone is talking about a balloon, a tyre, or an air mattress → filling with air.
  • If someone is very angry or emotions are running high → losing their temper.
  • If someone is talking about a photo or image → enlarging it.
  • If someone is talking about fame, a viral moment, or success → becoming very popular.
  • If someone is talking about a deal, a plan, or a relationship going wrong → failing completely.
  • If someone is talking about news or a story being exaggerated → making it seem bigger.
  • If someone's phone is involved → receiving lots of calls or messages.

"Blow up" can be separable. This means that when you use it with an object (a thing or person you are acting on), you can put that object either after "blow up" or between "blow" and "up."

Both of these are correct:

"She blew up the balloon." ✅
"She blew the balloon up." ✅

However, if you use a pronoun (like it, him, her, them), you must put the pronoun between "blow" and "up":

"She blew it up." ✅
"She blew up it." ❌
A Quick Summary of All Meanings

1. Explode — "The building blew up."
  2. Fill with air — "Blow up the balloon."
  3. Become very angry — "He blew up at me."
  4. Enlarge an image — "Blow up that photo."
  5. Become famous quickly — "She blew up overnight."
  6. Fail suddenly — "The deal blew up."
  7. Exaggerate — "The media blew up the story."
  8. Phone receiving many messages — "My phone is blowing up."

The best way to truly absorb "blow up" is to notice it whenever you read or listen to English. Each time you spot it, ask yourself: Which meaning is this? With practice, reading the context becomes second nature, and all these meanings will feel completely natural to you.
1906: A blowhard is a person who talks loudly and endlessly about how great, smart, knowledgeable, or important they are — but whose big talk is mostly empty air. The word captures two things at once: the volume of their talking and the hollowness behind it. Think of someone who is all bark and no bite, all show and no substance.

A blowhard:

  • Brags constantly. They talk about their own achievements, experiences, and opinions far more than any situation calls for. They find a way to make almost any conversation about themselves.
  • Exaggerates or inflates the truth. Their stories are always a little too impressive. That fish they caught keeps getting bigger every time they tell the story.
  • Acts like an authority on everything. They speak with great confidence about topics they don't actually know well. They give advice nobody asked for, and they never say "I don't know."
  • Dominates conversations. They are not really interested in listening. For them, a conversation is just an opportunity to perform.
  • Promises more than they deliver. If they say they can do something, there's a good chance they can't — or won't. Their words far outrun their actions.
The Single Most Important Thing to Understand

The heart of the word is this: there is a massive gap between what a blowhard says and what is actually true.

A confident person who backs up their words with real skill and action is not a blowhard. A person who genuinely knows a lot about a subject and shares that knowledge is not a blowhard. What makes someone a blowhard is precisely that their grand talk is not matched by reality. The louder and bigger the talk, the thinner the substance behind it.

"Blowhard" is always a negative and slightly mocking word. When you call someone a blowhard, you are not just describing them — you are criticising them and dismissing them. It carries a sense of "don't take this person too seriously." It's the kind of word people use with an eye-roll. It signals that the speaker finds the blowhard tiresome, ridiculous, or annoying.
How It Feels to Be Around a Blowhard

People find blowhards exhausting and irritating. You might feel:

  • Like you can never get a word in.
  • Bored or trapped, because the conversation goes nowhere real.
  • Slightly disrespected, because they clearly care more about talking than about you.
  • Quietly amused or contemptuous, because you can see through their exaggerations.

Over time, people stop trusting or taking blowhards seriously, even if they let them keep talking.

• "Nobody at the office believes his ideas anymore — he's just a blowhard who talks big but never follows through."
  • "She tuned him out halfway through dinner. He was such a blowhard, going on and on about how successful he was."
  • "Don't be fooled by him — he's a total blowhard. He's never actually done half the things he claims."
  • "The meeting was supposed to last an hour, but the blowhard in the corner turned it into a three-hour lecture about his own opinions."
How a Blowhard Differs From Similar Types of People

ConceptKey Difference

A liar deliberately says false things to deceive people for a specific goal. A blowhard may exaggerate and mislead too, but their primary drive is self-promotion and ego, not calculated deception.

A confident person believes in themselves and can usually back it up. A blowhard acts confident but is often masking insecurity beneath all that noise.

A loudmouth is simply someone who speaks too loudly or says inappropriate things. A blowhard is specifically about bragging and self-importance — it's more specific than just being loud.

A bore is someone who is dull and uninteresting. A blowhard can overlap with this, but the defining feature of a blowhard is the self-aggrandisement, not just the dullness.
Words That Are Close in Meaning

These words share the same spirit as "blowhard" and are worth knowing alongside it:

  • Braggart — someone who brags constantly (very close in meaning, but slightly more old-fashioned).
  • Windbag — someone who talks endlessly and says little of value (more emphasis on the length of talk, less on the bragging).
  • Boaster — someone who boasts about themselves (simpler, more neutral in tone).
  • Show-off — someone who tries to impress others by displaying their abilities or possessions (slightly less aggressive in tone than blowhard).

Of all these, blowhard is the most colourful and pointed — it combines the idea of too much hot air and too much ego in one sharp word.

If you had to boil it down to one sentence:

A blowhard is someone whose mouth is far bigger than their actual achievements — a loud, self-important talker who impresses themselves far more than they impress anyone else.

That's the word, fully understood.
1907:
"Blowing" as an adjective describes something that is being moved, carried, or driven through the air by wind — or something that is actively and noticeably producing or experiencing strong air movement.

It comes from the verb "blow," and when used as an adjective, it sits directly before a noun to describe that noun's current state of motion through air.
The main ways it is used

1. Something being carried or pushed by wind

This is the most common use. When you place "blowing" in front of a noun, it almost always means the wind has picked that thing up and is transporting it through the air.

  • blowing snow — snow that wind has lifted off the ground and is carrying through the air
  • blowing sand — grains of sand being pushed and swept by wind
  • blowing dust — fine dust lifted off the ground and moved through the air
  • blowing leaves — leaves being swept and tossed through the air by wind
  • blowing hair — hair being tossed and moved around by wind
  • blowing curtains — curtains billowing and moving because wind is pushing through them

In every case above, the word "blowing" tells you: this thing is not sitting still — wind is actively moving it.

2. Wind or air itself that is actively moving

"Blowing" can also describe wind or a force of air that is currently in action — moving, gusting, rushing.

  • a blowing wind — wind that is actively and noticeably moving at this moment
  • a blowing gale — a powerful, raging wind that is in full motion
  • a blowing breeze — a breeze that is currently flowing through the air

Here, "blowing" tells you the wind is not calm or still — it is live and in motion.

3. Anything producing a stream of air

More broadly, "blowing" can describe any source that is actively pushing or expelling air — not just natural wind, but anything that blows.

  • a blowing fan — a fan that is on and pushing air outward
  • a blowing vent — an air vent that is actively releasing air
A very important distinction — especially in weather

In weather reports and meteorology, "blowing" before certain words has a precise technical meaning worth knowing:

  • Blowing snow, blowing sand, and blowing dust are recognized weather events where wind lifts particles off the ground surface and carries them horizontally through the air, reducing visibility (how far you can see).

This is importantly different from related terms:

ConceptWhat it means
  • Falling snow means snow is coming down from clouds. Blowing snow means snow that already landed on the ground has been lifted back up by wind and is now being swept through the air again. It can be "blowing snow" even on a clear day with no snowfall, as long as wind is strong enough to pick up previously fallen snow.
  • Drifting snow stays low, near the ground, forming uneven piles (drifts). Blowing snow is lifted higher into the air, creating a hazy, white-out effect.

This distinction matters because blowing snow can be dangerous — it can reduce visibility to near zero without a single new snowflake falling from the sky.

The same logic applies to blowing dust and blowing sand: the particles are already on the ground, but powerful wind picks them up and launches them into the air.
How "blowing" is different from other similar adjectives

• Windy describes a place or time when there is a lot of wind in general: "It's a windy day." It describes the condition of the environment. "Blowing" describes something specific — a noun — that is actively being moved by that wind: "blowing leaves," "blowing sand."
  • Breezy is a softer, gentler version of windy — light, pleasant wind. "Blowing" implies more active, visible movement — something actually being lifted and carried.
  • Gusty describes wind that comes in sudden, irregular bursts. "Blowing" describes the state of something being in ongoing motion due to wind.
A note on "mind-blowing" and compound uses

You may also encounter "blowing" inside compound adjectives like mind-blowing. Here, the meaning has shifted figuratively: something that is "mind-blowing" is so surprising, impressive, or overwhelming that it figuratively "blows your mind" — it stuns you. But in this compound form, it's no longer about wind or air; it's entirely figurative. The standalone adjective "blowing" almost always connects back to the literal movement of air.
Quick mental test to recognize it

Whenever you see "blowing" before a noun, ask yourself: Is the wind — or some force of air — actively moving this thing right now? If yes, that is exactly what "blowing" is communicating. It signals live, active motion through air, rather than something calm, still, or settled.
1908: The word blowout is a single noun with several distinct meanings. Each meaning shares a common thread — something happening suddenly, forcefully, or on a very large scale. Here is every meaning explained clearly, with examples.
Meaning 1: A Tire That Suddenly Bursts

This is the most common, everyday meaning of the word.

A blowout happens when a vehicle's tire suddenly explodes or bursts while the vehicle is moving. It is not a slow, gradual loss of air — it is fast and loud, like a small explosion. This is dangerous because the driver can lose control of the vehicle.

"We were driving on the highway when we had a blowout. The car swerved and we had to pull over immediately."

"The blowout shredded the rear tire completely."

When people say "I had a blowout," most listeners immediately picture a burst tire. This meaning is used in everyday conversation all the time.
Meaning 2: A One-Sided Victory in Sports or Competition

In sports and competitive situations, a blowout refers to a game or contest where one side wins by a huge margin — so decisively that the result was never really in doubt. It is the opposite of a close, exciting match.

"The final score was 98 to 54. It was a complete blowout."

"Nobody wanted to watch the game after the first quarter — it had become a blowout."

The key idea here is that one team or side was so much stronger that the competition became almost meaningless. The word carries a slightly informal, conversational tone and is very common in sports commentary and casual talk.
Meaning 3: A Large, Lavish Party or Celebration

A blowout can also mean a big, extravagant celebration — a party or social event that is especially large, loud, or expensive. The "blow" here suggests going all-out, sparing no effort.

"They threw a massive blowout for her retirement — there were hundreds of guests and a live band."

"We're planning a real blowout for New Year's Eve this year."

This meaning is casual and positive. It suggests the event was memorable, over-the-top, or particularly lively. You often see phrases like "throw a blowout" or "have a blowout."

In the context of hair and beauty, a blowout refers to a professional hair treatment where a stylist washes your hair and then blow-dries and brushes it to make it look smooth, voluminous, and styled. No cutting involved — it is purely about styling using heat and a brush.

"She got a blowout before the wedding so her hair would look perfectly straight and shiny."

"I go to the salon every two weeks just for a blowout."

This meaning is very common, especially in American English. Many salons offer "blowouts" as a quick, affordable service compared to a full haircut appointment.
Meaning 5: An Uncontrolled Burst from an Oil or Gas Well

In the oil and gas industry, a blowout is a serious industrial accident where oil, gas, or both suddenly and violently burst out of a well in an uncontrolled way. This happens when the pressure underground is too great to be contained. Blowouts can cause fires, explosions, and major environmental disasters.

"The offshore blowout spilled millions of gallons of oil into the sea."

"Engineers worked for weeks trying to stop the blowout."

This is a technical, industry-specific meaning, but it appears often in news reporting about energy and environmental disasters.
Meaning 6: A Blown Fuse or Electrical Failure

A blowout can describe the sudden failure of an electrical component — most commonly a fuse — due to excess electricity passing through it. When a fuse blows, it cuts off the power to protect equipment. This is sometimes called a blowout because the fuse is designed to "blow" (break open) under overload.

"There was a blowout in the circuit, and half the lights in the building went dark."

"The power surge caused a blowout, and we had to replace several fuses."

This meaning is less common in daily conversation but appears in technical and household contexts.

Particularly in retail, a blowout (sometimes written as blowout sale) refers to a large sale where a store tries to sell off all its remaining inventory, often at very low prices. The goal is to "blow out" (clear out) all the stock quickly.

"The store is closing down — everything is half price in the blowout sale."

"They're having a blowout on last season's electronics."

This meaning is common in advertising and retail contexts.

Even though the contexts differ wildly — tires, sports, parties, hair, oil wells — the word blowout always suggests something happening in a big, sudden, or extreme way. A tire doesn't slowly deflate — it blows out violently. A sports result isn't close — it's overwhelmingly one-sided. A party isn't modest — it's extravagant. This shared sense of "excessive force or scale" is the invisible thread running through all uses of the word.

• Someone talking about driving → burst tire
  • Someone talking about a game or match → one-sided result
  • Someone talking about a party or event → big celebration
  • Someone talking about hair → blow-dry styling session
  • Someone talking about oil or energy → uncontrolled well eruption
  • Someone talking about electricity → blown fuse or power failure
  • Someone talking about shopping → clearance sale
1909:
Blubber is the thick, soft layer of fat that sits just beneath the skin of certain sea animals — most famously whales, but also seals, walruses, and dolphins.

Think of it like a built-in coat. Just as you wear a thick winter jacket to survive freezing cold weather, these animals have blubber wrapped all around their bodies to survive freezing cold ocean water. Except unlike your jacket, blubber is not worn — it is a part of their body, sandwiched between their outer skin and their inner muscles.

Blubber is not just any ordinary fat. It is a dense, thick, oily layer of fatty tissue. In large whales, this layer can be anywhere from a few centimetres to over 50 centimetres (nearly 20 inches) thick. If you were to cut through a whale, you would see a distinct, pale yellowish-white rubbery layer — that is the blubber.

It feels soft and greasy, much like the fat you might see around a cut of meat, but far thicker and more organised as a continuous layer all over the animal's body.

Blubber serves three major purposes, and understanding these will make the word stick in your mind forever.

1. It keeps the animal warm (insulation)
Ocean water — especially in the Arctic or deep sea — is bitterly cold. If a whale had no blubber, the cold water would drain heat from its body very quickly, just like how standing outside without a jacket in winter makes you cold fast. Blubber traps the animal's body heat inside, acting as a near-perfect insulator. The thicker the blubber, the better protected the animal is from the cold.

2. It stores energy (fuel reserve)
Fat is a form of stored energy. When a whale travels thousands of miles during migration and cannot eat for weeks or even months, its body slowly burns through its blubber for fuel — the same way a car burns through its petrol tank on a long road trip.

3. It helps the animal float (buoyancy)
Fat is lighter than muscle and bone, so blubber makes the animal slightly more buoyant (easier to float) in water. This is helpful for animals that spend their entire lives in the ocean.

Blubber forms a complete layer all around the animal's body — like a full-body suit under the skin. It covers the top, bottom, and sides, but is usually not found in the fins or tail flukes. This uniform coverage is important so that no part of the animal's body loses heat to the water.

In its most proper and common use, blubber refers specifically to this fat layer in marine (sea-dwelling) mammals. You would not usually say that a land animal like a bear or a pig has "blubber" — those animals have fat, but the word blubber is reserved for sea animals.

However, in informal, everyday conversation — especially among children or in casual speech — blubber is sometimes used to refer to excess body fat on a human being, usually in a rude or teasing way (e.g., "Look at all that blubber on him"). This usage is considered unkind and insulting. You should be aware it exists, but know that using it this way about a person is disrespectful.

For hundreds of years, people hunted whales primarily for their blubber. When blubber is boiled down, it produces a rich oil (called whale oil) that was once used as fuel in oil lamps to light homes, as a lubricant for machinery, and as an ingredient in soap and candles. This made whale blubber an extremely valuable and heavily traded commodity — before petroleum and electricity became widely available. Today, commercial whaling for blubber is banned or heavily restricted in most of the world.

What it isA thick layer of fat beneath the skin
Found inWhales, seals, walruses, dolphins, and similar sea mammals
Main jobsKeep the animal warm, store energy, aid in floating
AppearanceSoft, pale yellowish-white, oily, and dense
In informal useRudely refers to excess body fat on a person
A Sentence to Remember It By

"The whale's thick blubber kept it perfectly warm even in the icy Arctic waters, despite the temperature being just a few degrees above freezing."

After reading this, if someone mentions blubber in any context — a nature documentary, a history book about whale hunters, or even a rude playground comment — you will know exactly what it means, where it comes from, and why it matters.
